then.text: Off back north? Dreckly, as we say. It means 'eventually', and it's how long the trains take.

else.text: An End to End card from John o' Groats? Proper job! I'm the stamp at this end. Land's End is just along the road, but the road's shut, so here'll do.
But nobody gets a stamp from me without a race. I did the whole thing on a bike in nine days, and my team did it in a basket. Let's see yours.

then.text: The End to Ender stamps your card with a tiny engine house and a pasty, then signs it with a flourish.
Now take it back to the clerk at John o' Groats. 874 miles. Don't forget to wave at Bristol.

rail_guard.text: Penzance. The end of the line. Past here there's only the sea and a gentle sense of finality.
Hop aboard. The Wildlore rail runs to any town you have visited. Where to?

pasty_baker.text: A Cornish pasty was a miner's lunch: the thick crimped edge was a handle, so dirty hands didn't touch the food. They threw the crust away.
I never throw the crust away. It's the best bit. Some say you should leave it for the knockers. I say that's a different kind of lunch.

then.text: Mist rolling in off the moor. The knockers like a foggy day, so they say. Leave a crust out.
Rain don't bother a miner. Forty years underground, I did. Weather's a treat.

old_miner.text: The knockers are small folk who tapped at the rock, so the story goes. Miners left a bit of pasty crust for them, for luck.
I'm told they were harmless. But if you whistled underground, they'd come and complain.

mount_ferryman.text: The causeway is 'pass at your own risk' for about two hours either side of low tide.
Between those, I'll ferry you across. Fifteen quid. Splash included.

then.text: Waves are coming right over the pool wall today. Free extra sea. I'll still go in. Dreckly.
Raining? I'm getting wet anyway, my love. Makes no difference to me.
Dawn dip! The sun comes up over Mount's Bay and you forget your toes have gone numb. Mostly.

lido_swimmer.text: {greeting} The Jubilee Pool is a seawater lido. It's cold. I'll swim all year. It's good for you. I'm told. I can't feel my toes to check.
They heat part of it with a geothermal well now. It's 'warmish', which is as warm as Cornwall gets.

then.text: Sun on Market Jew Street, and the Davy statue looks very pleased with himself. As he should.
Lamps coming on at dusk. Every time I see a lamp, I think of Davy. I'm great fun at parties.

davy_fan.text: Sir Humphry Davy invented the safety lamp in 1815. The flame was shrouded in wire mesh, so it couldn't set off firedamp in the mine.
He never patented it. He said he wanted to help miners, not make money. A very unfashionable idea.

then.text: Gale's up, so the Scillonian's staying put. You'll get to Scilly dreckly, my bird. Have a pasty.
Fog in the bay. Can't see St Michael's Mount, but I promise it's still there. It's mostly rock.

harbour_master.text: Penzance is the biggest town in Penwith. And the sea gets in everywhere. It's a lifestyle.
The Scillonian ferry leaves from this quay for the Isles of Scilly. There's a lot of sea to cross, and a lot of sandwiches to eat.

landsky_drift.text: Dydh da! Mind the palms. They're not palms, strictly, they're cabbage trees from New Zealand, but everybody calls them Cornish palms and the palms don't mind.

People ask how they survive. We're as far north as Labrador, where the sea freezes. The answer's out there: the Gulf Stream brings warm water up from the Gulf of Mexico, and the North Atlantic Drift carries it across to wash our coast. The sea round here never gets properly cold, so neither does the air.

It's why Edinburgh is milder in winter than Moscow at the same latitude, and why Tresco over on Scilly has a garden full of plants from South Africa and Australia. Inverewe, way up in Wester Ross, grows them too. Same warm water, further on.

The scientists watch that current closely. As the world warms the whole Atlantic circulation is expected to weaken, and if it did much, a lot of us would be buying coats. Tell the forecaster at Exeter the palms are fine. For now.

ct_bodmin_towels.text: Beast of Bodmin tea towels, three for a tenner. Nobody's seen it in years, and that's very good for trade. Mind, Jory won't buy one.

ct_bodmin_barns.text: The flocks come in at dusk now. It's a nuisance, but it works. Whatever it was has gone off to bother Somerset.

then.text: Somebody caught the Beast of Bodmin, they say, and put it in a team. I told them it was a hoax. I'm wrong, aren't I?

else.text: They took the Beast off in a lorry with the blinds down. The moor's never been so quiet. The pub's never been so empty.
